Predict, compare, and update only on a mistake.

Source context:
Every weight of the KP01 neuron had to be worked out by hand. Rosenblatt's idea of 1958 adds feedback: for each sample, compute the sum $s$, pass it through the step to get $o_i$, and compare with the correct label $y_i$; if right, do nothing; if wrong, push the weights one step in the right direction. This is a **supervised** rule, driven by labels and mistakes, essentially different from classical Hebbian learning (neurons that fire together strengthen their link).

An update improves this sample’s score direction, not every sample. Rate-scaling equivalence needs zero starts and consistent order/ties; batch and sequential trajectories can differ.

Symbols:
$\mathbf{x}_i$: the $i$-th input, with $x_{i0}=1$ added (bias folded into $\mathbf{w}$)
$y_i\in\{0,1\}$: correct label of the $i$-th sample
$o_i=f(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_i)$: output under the current weights, with $f$ the step of KP01
$\eta>0$: learning rate: the size of one correction
$y_i-o_i$: error, which can only be $0$, $+1$ or $-1$

steps.label: A batch sums the corrections before one update · 1
steps.speakerNotes:
Previously: Added: fixed order and zero start give the same predictions.

A batch evaluates all outputs and errors under the same old weights, sums the correction terms, and updates once. Sequential processing can change weights between samples, so a multi-sample batch generally differs from sequential updates. A batch of one reduces directly to the single-sample rule.

Source context:
$$
\mathbf{w}\leftarrow\mathbf{w}+\eta\,(y_i-o_i)\,\mathbf{x}_i
$$

The direction is always right: after the update $s'=\mathbf{w}'^\top\mathbf{x}_i=s+\eta(y_i-o_i)\|\mathbf{x}_i\|^2$, and $x_{i0}=1$ makes $\|\mathbf{x}_i\|^2\ge1$. So $s$ rises when the error is $+1$ and falls when it is $-1$. You can also look at a batch of $b$ samples before updating: $\mathbf{w}\leftarrow\mathbf{w}+\eta\sum_{i=1}^{b}(y_i-o_i)\mathbf{x}_i$; $b=1$ is the one-at-a-time version.

An update improves this sample’s score direction, not every sample. Rate-scaling equivalence needs zero starts and consistent order/ties; batch and sequential trajectories can differ.
